Complete Blocking-Flow Theory ​

Source page ID: vpdiGyjNPuVu69MdSigFsV ｜ Open in Tencent Docs

1　Precise Definition of the Original Model ​

1.1　Graph Definition ​

Let G=(V,E) be a directed graph, with n=|V| and m=|E|. Parallel edges are allowed. Write δ−(v) and δ+(v) for the sets of edges entering and leaving v. A self-loop appears once in each set and therefore cancels in the conservation equation.

Node types are determined entirely by indegree and outdegree:

TypeIndegreeOutdegreeNotation
Source depot01W+
Destination depot10W−
Splitter11, 2, or 3S
Converger2 or 31M

If any other node type exists, the input is invalid according to the specification. We discuss only valid graphs below. Let I=S∪M, W=W+∪W−, k=|I|, and w=|W|. The set of depot-adjacent edges is

B={e=(u,v)∈E:u∈W+ or v∈W−}.

An edge directly connecting a source depot to a destination depot is counted in B only once. Define the boundary projection PBx=(xe)e∈B, with coordinates ordered by the original edge numbering.

1.2　Flow and Conservation Rules ​

Every edge satisfies 0<xe≤1. Ordinary nodes satisfy

∑e∈δ−(v)xe=∑e∈δ+(v)xe,v∈I.

Each group of parallel edges sharing the same start and end nodes has equal flow. Write the set of candidate fixed edges as

C={(u,v)∈E:u∈W+∪M, v∈W−∪S}.

Write F for the fixed-edge set. We require

xe=1(e∈F),xe<1(e∈C, e∉F).

Other nonfixed edges still satisfy xe≤1. An edge that is neither a candidate nor fixed may have flow 1.

Automatic mode requires ∅≠F⊆C. Explicit mode requires F=F∗, where F∗ is a nonempty edge set supplied in the input and may contain noncandidate edges. We return to this later.

1.3　Buffer States and Propagation Rules ​

Each edge has state σe and two Boolean quantities ιe and ωe:

Stateιe (can_in)ωe (can_out)
EMPTY10
FULL01
PARTIAL11

Only edges starting in S and ending in M may be PARTIAL. A source depot's output edge must be FULL; nonfixed edges entering destination depots must be EMPTY.

For splitter v, denote its unique input edge by p(v). For converger v, denote its unique output edge by q(v). Define propagation conditions by

e,p(v)∉F ⟹ (ιe⇒ιp(v)),e∈δ+(v), v∈S,e,q(v)∉F ⟹ (ωe⇒ωq(v)),e∈δ−(v), v∈M.

Propagation applies only to the relevant nonfixed edges. However, imposing additional propagation conditions on fixed edges can only reduce the valid-solution set; this article's invariance conclusion remains true for the remaining valid solutions.

Note that p(v) ends at a splitter and q(v) starts at a converger, so neither can be PARTIAL.

1.4　Local Maximum Rules ​

For a nonfixed output edge of splitter v, whenever ιe=1,

xe≥xffor all f∈δ+(v), f∉F.

For a nonfixed input edge of converger v, whenever ωe=1,

xe≥xffor all f∈δ−(v), f∉F.

Consequently, two locally maximal nonfixed edges in the same direction at the same node necessarily have equal flow.

1.5　Basic Configurations and Full-Rank Valid Solutions ​

Definition 1.1 (Basic feasible configuration). A triple (x,F,σ) satisfying all conditions in 1.1–1.4 is a basic feasible configuration. Denote its set of flow vectors by X0.

Definition 1.2 (Full-rank valid solution). For a basic feasible configuration, combine the conservation equations, parallel-edge equal-flow equations, fixed-edge equations, and selected equal-flow equations into Ax=b, and require rankA=m. A configuration satisfying this condition is a valid solution; denote its flow set by Xval.

Immediately, Xval⊆X0. We first prove the stronger conclusion that boundary invariance holds over all of X0. Thus neither the choice of local actions nor the full-rank requirement is a hidden premise of the proof.

2　Two Necessary Structural Lemmas ​

Lemma 2.1　Through-Flow and Fixed Branches ​

For any basic feasible configuration and any v∈I, define

tv=∑e∈δ−(v)xe=∑e∈δ+(v)xe.

Then 0<tv≤1. Every output edge of a splitter with at least two outputs is nonfixed and has flow strictly below 1. Every input edge of a converger is likewise nonfixed and has flow strictly below 1.

Proof. A splitter's through-flow equals its unique input-edge flow, and a converger's through-flow equals its unique output-edge flow, so 0<tv≤1. If a branch group containing at least two edges had an edge with flow 1, the strictly positive flows of its other edges would make the sum exceed 1, contradicting tv≤1. Fixed edges have flow 1, so such a group contains no fixed edge. ∎

Lemma 2.2　Rationality and Output Length of Valid Solutions ​

Every coordinate of a full-rank valid solution is rational. If xe=pe/de is a reduced positive fraction, then

1≤pe≤de≤2m.

Proof. Select m independent rows of A, obtaining an invertible integer matrix A′ and integer right-hand side b′. Each conservation row has at most four nonzero coefficients, all ±1; canceling self-loops cannot increase its norm. A fixed-edge row has Euclidean norm 1, and a parallel-edge or local equal-flow row has norm 2. Hence every row has norm at most 2. Hadamard's inequality gives 1≤|detA′|≤2m. By Cramer's rule, each reduced denominator divides |detA′|. The numerator bound follows from 0<xe≤1. ∎

Thus each flow has an O(m)-bit numerator and denominator, and the explicit binary representation of the entire flow vector has length O(m2).

3　Auxiliary Model ​

3.1　Definition of the Auxiliary Model ​

Let H=(L⊔R,E) be a finite bipartite graph. Every edge has positive capacity ce, and every vertex has positive quota Qv. Each vertex partitions its incident edges into nonempty ordered groups

Πv=(πv1,…,πvsv),

where a smaller group index means higher priority and edges in the same group have equal priority. Write jv(e) for the index of the group containing edge e.

For a local request vector z, with 0≤ze≤ce, define the acceptance operator Cv as follows. If ∑eze≤Qv, accept everything. Otherwise let h be the first group whose cumulative request reaches Qv, and let

r=Qv−∑j<h∑e∈πvjze>0.

Choose a truncation height λ satisfying ∑e∈πvhmin(ze,λ)=r, and set

(Cv(z))e=ze,jv(e)<h;(Cv(z))e=min(ze,λ),jv(e)=h;(Cv(z))e=0,jv(e)>h.

Within 0≤λ≤maxe∈πvhze, the required height is unique: the left side is continuous and strictly increasing until it reaches the group's total request. If the cumulative request equals the quota exactly, take the group's maximum request as the height; the acceptance vector is still unique.

Definition 3.1 (Feasible assignment, willingness to increase, blocking, and stability). A vector y is a feasible assignment if 0≤ye≤ce and each vertex's total incident assignment does not exceed Qv. For ye<ce, if some 0<ε≤ce−ye satisfies

(Cv(yv+ε1e))e>ye,

we say vertex v is willing to increase edge e. A capacity-saturated edge cannot increase. An edge is blocking if both endpoints are willing to increase it. A feasible assignment with no blocking edge is stable.

Lemma 3.2　Necessary and Sufficient Conditions for Willingness to Increase ​

Suppose y is feasible and ye<ce.

If ∑fyf<Qv, then v is willing to increase every unsaturated edge. If the total equals Qv, let h be the last group containing positive flow and let λ=maxf∈πvhyf. Then

v is willing to increase e⟺jv(e)<h or (jv(e)=h and ye<λ).

Proof. If the quota is not filled, choose ε smaller than both the remaining quota and the remaining edge capacity; the increase is accepted in full.

Now suppose the quota is filled. Since Qv>0, h exists and λ>0.

If jv(e)<h, choose the increase smaller than the total in the last positive-flow group. The earlier cumulative amount remains insufficient to use the entire quota, so the increase is accepted in full and group h bears the reduction.

If jv(e)=h and ye<λ, choose positive ε smaller than the remaining edge capacity, λ, and (λ−ye)/2. After increasing the request, the new height λ′ for group h lies in [λ−ε,λ]. At height λ, that group's total increases by ε; lowering the height to λ−ε removes at least ε from at least one formerly maximal edge. Since ye+ε<λ−ε≤λ′, the entire additional request on e is retained. Thus the vertex is willing to increase it.

If jv(e)=h and ye=λ, any permitted positive increase leaves the vector truncated at height λ unchanged. This height still exactly fills the remaining quota, so the accepted amount on e remains λ=ye. The vertex is unwilling to increase it.

If jv(e)>h, all groups up to h already fill the quota. Increasing a request in a later group cannot change that fact, and the entire increase is rejected. These four cases exhaust the possibilities. ∎

Proposition 3.3　Item-by-Item Equivalence to Karzanov v2 ​

The SMP model in Section 2 of reference [1] and the auxiliary model of Section 3.1 are identical on the same bipartite simple graph.

Theorem 3.4　Results from the Literature ​

For the mixed-choice-function model on the finite bipartite simple graph above, we use these proved results: stable assignments exist; each vertex's total incident assignment is the same in all stable assignments; an exact polynomial-time stable-assignment algorithm exists. The first two are restated in equation (2.7), pages 9–10 of [1], explicitly attributed there to Alkan–Gale [3]. Vertex-total invariance is equation (2.7)(b). The polynomial algorithm for the mixed-choice model used here appears in Appendix A, pages 35–38 of [1], Proposition A.1 (page 38). The complexity model and intermediate-data lengths are discussed on page 4.

4　Auxiliary Bipartite Graph ​

4.1　Construction ​

Construct H with left and right sides

L={vout:v∈I}∪W+,R={vin:v∈I}∪W−.

For each original edge e=(u,v), add an edge eH of capacity 1. Its left endpoint is the ordinary node's uout or source depot u; its right endpoint is the ordinary node's vin or destination depot v.

For every v∈I, add two distinctly numbered auxiliary edges av,bv between vout and vin, each of capacity 4. Give every auxiliary-graph vertex quota 4. Specify

Πvout=({av},{eH:e∈δ+(v)},{bv}),Πvin=({bv},{eH:e∈δ−(v)},{av}).

Each depot has just one priority group, consisting of its unique incident edge. The original model's parallel-edge flow equality will be preserved in the embedding; auxiliary edges are not subject to that restriction.

There are 2k+w vertices and m+2k edges.

Lemma 4.1　Two Operating Configurations of an Auxiliary Node ​

Suppose the total original input and output are both t, with 0<t≤1. Two feasible local configurations are

Type A: yav=4−t, ybv=0;Type B: yav=0, ybv=4−t.

In type A, the input side is willing to increase every unsaturated original input edge, while the output side rejects precisely the maximum-flow edges in the original output group. In type B, the output side is willing to increase every unsaturated original output edge, while the input side rejects precisely the maximum-flow edges in the original input group. Neither configuration has blocking auxiliary edges.

Proof. Both endpoints have total assignment 4. In type A, the output side's last positive group is the original output group, so Lemma 3.2 says that among unsaturated edges, precisely the locally maximal ones are rejected. The input side's last positive group is the lowest-priority group {av}; all original inputs precede it, so it is willing to increase every unsaturated original input.

Auxiliary edge av is maximal in the input side's last positive group and is therefore rejected there; bv comes after the output side's last positive group and is rejected there. Neither auxiliary edge blocks. Type B exchanges the endpoints and auxiliary edges, with the same argument: the input side's critical group is the original input group, and the output side's critical group is {bv}; the output side rejects bv and the input side rejects av. ∎

5　Embedding Original Configurations into Stable Assignments ​

Theorem 5.1　Stable Embedding Preserving Original-Edge Flows ​

Every basic feasible configuration (x,F,σ) extends to a stable assignment y on H with yeH=xe.

Construction. Select each ordinary node's type by the following rules, then put its remaining quota 4−tv on the auxiliary edge specified in Lemma 4.1.

Original nodeConditionAuxiliary configuration
Splitter vp(v)∈F, or σp(v)= EMPTYType A
Splitter vp(v)∉F and σp(v)= FULLType B
Converger vq(v)∉F and σq(v)= EMPTYType A
Converger vq(v)∈F, or σq(v)= FULLType B

The single-branch edge cannot be PARTIAL, so the cases are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. A fixed single-branch edge's state does not affect this construction.

Step one: feasibility. Set yeH=xe on original edges, respecting capacity 1. By Lemma 2.1, the positive auxiliary amount 4−tv belongs to [3,4) and respects capacity 4. Both copies of every ordinary node exactly fill quota 4. Each depot has only one capacity-1 edge, giving total at most 1 and hence respecting quota 4. Thus y is feasible.

Step two: auxiliary edges do not block. By Lemma 4.1, at least one endpoint rejects each auxiliary edge.

Step three: original edges do not block. If xe=1, the corresponding edge is saturated and cannot block. We therefore consider only xe<1. Since fixed edges have flow 1, necessarily e∉F. Proceed by state.

Case E: σe= EMPTY, where e=(u,v). Then ιe=1, and u cannot be a source depot. If u∈S and p(u) is fixed, the table assigns u type A. If p(u) is nonfixed, both edges are nonfixed and propagation gives ιp(u)=1. This input cannot be PARTIAL, so it is EMPTY, again assigning u type A. The local maximum rule and Lemma 2.1 show that e is maximal in the entire output group. Lemma 4.1 therefore ensures the output side rejects eH. If u∈M, then e=q(u) is that converger's unique output. It is nonfixed and EMPTY, so u has type A. Its sole output is automatically maximal, and the output side again rejects eH.

Case F: σe= FULL. Since e is nonfixed, v cannot be a destination depot. If v∈M and q(v) is fixed, v has type B. If q(v) is nonfixed, ωe=1 and propagation give ωq(v)=1; this output cannot be PARTIAL, so it is FULL, again assigning v type B. The local maximum rule and Lemma 2.1 show e is maximal in the entire input group, so the input side rejects eH. If v∈S, then e=p(v) is a nonfixed FULL input and v has type B. Its sole input is automatically maximal, so the input side rejects eH.

Case P: σe= PARTIAL. By definition u∈S, v∈M, and ιe=ωe=1. Repeat the splitter argument from case E at the output side and the converger argument from case F at the input side. Both sides reject eH.

These three cases exhaust all unsaturated original edges. At least one endpoint rejects every edge, so there is no blocking edge and y is stable. ∎

6　Eliminating Parallel Edges ​

Lemma 6.1　Multiplicity Bound ​

At most three edges connect any pair of endpoints in H.

Proof. For endpoint pairs without auxiliary edges, all edges come from a single ordered endpoint pair in the original graph. Their multiplicity is at most the original node's outdegree, hence at most 3. For the pair vout,vin, the only possible edge besides the two auxiliary edges comes from an original self-loop. A valid ordinary node has degree 1 in at least one direction, so there is at most one such self-loop. The total is still at most 3. ∎

6.1　Threefold Cover ​

Replace every vertex z of H with (z,0),(z,1),(z,2), taking copy indices modulo 3. For each pair of endpoints ℓ∈L,r∈R, give their connecting edges distinct labels d(e)∈{0,1,2}. For each edge e=ℓr, add three edges

ei=((ℓ,i),(r,i+d(e))),i∈Z/3Z.

Every edge copy inherits its original capacity, and every vertex copy inherits its original quota. At each vertex copy, every original incident edge occurs exactly once. Inherit all priority groups through this natural bijection.

Lemma 6.2　Preservation of Definitions ​

H~ is a bipartite simple graph, and each vertex copy's acceptance operator differs from the original vertex's operator only by coordinate renaming.

Proof. Every edge still connects a left copy to a right copy, so the graph is bipartite and loopless. Distinct edges of the same original endpoint pair have different labels; thus for a fixed left copy i, they connect to different right copies. Different original endpoint pairs cannot produce the same copy endpoint pair, and different i for the same original edge have different left endpoints. Hence there are no parallel edges.

At a left copy, incident edges obviously correspond bijectively to the original incident edges. At right copy (r,j), original edge e=ℓr corresponds to the unique i=j−d(e), again giving a bijection. It preserves capacities, quotas, and every priority group, so the within-group sums, minimum operations, and truncation heights in the acceptance formulas are preserved exactly. ∎

Lemma 6.3　Stable Lifting ​

If y is a stable assignment on H, define y~ei=ye. Then y~ is stable on H~.

Proof. Each vertex copy has the same list of incident flows as the original vertex, satisfying every capacity and quota constraint. By Lemma 6.2, a vertex copy is willing to increase ei exactly when the corresponding original vertex is willing to increase e. If both ends of a copied edge were willing to increase it, both ends of the original edge would be too, contradicting stability of y. ∎

The covering graph therefore strictly satisfies the graph-type requirements of Proposition 3.3 and external Theorem 3.4. Its size is

|V(H~)|=3(2k+w),|E(H~)|=3(m+2k).

Every depot copy still has only one capacity-1 edge. An original depot-adjacent edge has endpoint-pair multiplicity 1 in H, so its label can be fixed at 0. Its zeroth copy then joins the corresponding zeroth endpoints, making results easy to read.

7　Main Theorem: Uniqueness of Depot-Edge Flows ​

Theorem 7.1　Boundary Invariance of Basic Feasible Configurations ​

Fix a valid directed topology G. Any two basic feasible configurations (x,F,σ) and (x′,F′,σ′) satisfy

PBx=PBx′.

Proof. Theorem 5.1 produces stable assignments y,y′ on H, agreeing with x,x′ respectively on original-edge coordinates. Since the construction of H depends only on G, both belong to the same auxiliary instance. Lemma 6.3 yields two stable assignments y~,y~′ on the same bipartite simple graph H~.

Take any boundary edge e∈B, a depot endpoint z, and its zeroth copy. This copy has degree 1, so its total incident assignment is y~e0H=xe, and under the other assignment y~e0H′=xe′. Proposition 3.3 and Lemma 6.2 ensure that stability on the covering graph exactly matches the paper's definition. Vertex-total invariance from external Theorem 3.4 therefore applies directly, giving xe=xe′. Repeat for every e∈B. ∎

If B=∅, both sides are empty vectors and the conclusion still holds.

Corollary 7.2　Boundary Uniqueness of the Original Solver's Valid Solutions ​

If Xval≠∅, a unique vector β(G) exists such that

PBx=β(G)for every x∈Xval.

Proof. Valid solutions form a subset of basic configurations. Existence follows by projecting any valid solution; uniqueness follows from Theorem 7.1. ∎

A fixed-edge mode merely filters basic configurations. Thus, on the same topology, changing the valid fixed-edge set does not change depot flows whenever the corresponding valid solutions exist. This does not imply that every fixed-edge set admits a solution.

Corollary 7.3　Differences Between Solutions Lie Only in the Internal Cycle Space ​

Let D be the full directed incidence matrix, including depot rows, with −1 at each edge's start and +1 at its end. The difference h=x−x′ between any two basic flows satisfies

Dh=0,he=0(e∈B).

Proof. For ordinary-node rows, subtract the two conservation equations. Each depot has just one incident edge, whose difference is zero by Theorem 7.1. Thus every node row is zero. ∎

This is a signed-cycle-space statement; it does not require the original directed graph to contain a directed cycle. Choose a spanning forest of the underlying undirected graph. Each nontree edge generates a fundamental cycle. Successively subtract the corresponding signed cycle vectors according to their nontree-edge coordinates. The remaining conserved vector is supported on the forest; applying conservation from the leaves inward shows it is zero. Hence h is a linear combination of these internal fundamental-cycle vectors.

8　Exact Polynomial-Time Computation of Depot-Edge Flows ​

Theorem 8.1　Polynomial Algorithm ​

The input is a valid topology and a fixed-edge mode permitted by the specification, with a promise that at least one valid solution exists. An algorithm can exactly output all depot-adjacent flows in time polynomial in the input length. In fact, the weaker promise that a basic feasible configuration exists already suffices for correct boundary output.

Algorithm. Construct H as in Section 4 and H~ as in Section 6. Invoke the exact stable-assignment algorithm from external Theorem 3.4 on H~, obtaining any stable assignment z. For each original boundary edge e, output its zeroth-copy value ze0H.

Correctness proof. By the existence promise, choose an original valid solution x. Theorem 5.1 and Lemma 6.3 give a stable assignment y~ on the same covering graph with y~e0H=xe. The algorithm's z is another stable assignment of this instance. Each depot copy has degree 1; vertex-total invariance gives ze0H=y~e0H=xe. By Corollary 7.2, this is the flow of that edge in every valid solution. ∎

Complexity proof. Every valid node has total degree at most 4, so m≤2n. Even without this bound, both auxiliary vertex and edge counts are O(n+m). Grouping original edges, adding auxiliary edges, and constructing the threefold cover all take polynomial time. Hash tables allow expected linear-time construction; sorting permits construction in O((n+m)log⁡(n+m)) comparisons.

The covering graph's capacities are only 1 or 4, all quotas are 4, and priorities have at most three levels. The binary length of endpoint identifiers and all priority lists is O((n+m)log⁡(n+m)).

Let the literature algorithm's operation bound for an instance with N vertices and M edges be polynomial p(N,M). Page 4 of [1] also states that intermediate data have polynomial storage length for integer capacity/quota inputs; Appendix A, Proposition A.1, supplies the polynomial algorithm. Thus both operation count and rational bit lengths are bounded polynomially in this instance's input size. Exact rational arithmetic consequently gives polynomial time in the usual binary model. Reading at most m coordinates at the end is also polynomial. ∎

References ​

[1] Alexander V. Karzanov. On stable assignments generated by choice functions of mixed type. arXiv:2401.11556v2, revised May 21, 2024, 39 pages. arXiv v2; Paper PDF.

[2] Tamás Fleiner. On stable matchings and flows. EGRES Technical Report 2009-11, 2009. Paper PDF.

[3] A. Alkan and D. Gale. Stable schedule matching under revealed preference. Journal of Economic Theory 112 (2003), 289–306.
